analysis: A cast bronze lady's hand, and the third photograph settles it completely: the flat wrist face is struck 'F. BARBEDIENNE' in the correct arched foundry mark. Ferdinand Barbedienne ran the most important art-bronze foundry in 19th-century Paris, and a struck foundry mark of this kind is the single most reliable attribution available in decorative bronze -- far better evidence than an artist signature, which can be cast in. The hand itself supports the date: solid cast, naturalistic modelling, a warm brown patina rubbed lighter at the knuckles and fingertips exactly where a desk object gets handled. Catalogued c.1850. This hits the antique criterion and the named-maker criterion at once, which very little in this sale does, and it lands inside the band.
problems: The catalogue misspells the foundry as 'Barbidienne', which will cost it search traffic and is worth knowing about -- it means fewer people find the lot. Barbedienne cast for seventy years and the mark alone does not date a piece within that range; c.1850 is the catalogue's claim, not evidence. Cast hands were made as paperweights and as parts, so establish that this is a complete finished object and not a fragment off a larger figure -- the flat, finished, struck wrist face argues it is complete. At $500-700 estimate this is $660-924 all-in, near the top of the band, so there is not much room if it runs.
patience: Low to moderate. Marked Barbedienne bronzes appear regularly, but almost always as figures well above this budget; the small desk objects are where the name is affordable.

analysis: A circa 1780 engraving of New Zealand chiefs and a war canoe -- almost certainly a plate from the published accounts of Cook's voyages, which were issued in London from 1773 and are the foundational images of Pacific exploration. Catalogued to c.1780, so it is one of a handful of genuinely 18th-century objects in the sale, and at $300-500 it is inside the band with room. The war-canoe subject gives it a real connection to the marine material this collection is building.
problems: Cook voyage plates were reissued and pirated throughout the 19th century, and later French and German editions used re-engraved copies of the same images; establishing a first-edition London plate needs the platemark, the paper and the engraver's line examined out of the frame. Loose plates are usually trimmed, and trimming into the platemark halves the value. No engraver, publisher or voyage named in the title -- that is the work to do at preview.
patience: Moderate. Cook voyage plates run steadily in book and map sales; the canoe and chief subjects are among the more sought.

analysis: A bronze bell on an iron swing bracket, catalogued 19th century. The bell is the good part: a proper cast profile with turned rings at the lip and a fine, even, genuinely developed green verdigris that has not been applied. The iron yoke is pierced and has its crank handle, and reads as period wrought and cast work. A handsome, useful, honestly old object.
problems: The wooden base is a later display mounting -- old weathered timber, but the hex nuts and washers holding the standards down are modern. That is a mount rather than a fault, but it means the assembly as sold is not an intact original. No founder's mark mentioned; check the crown and the inside of the lip for one, since a marked American bell (Meneely, Blake, Buckeye) is worth two to three times an unmarked one. At $600-800 the estimate runs ahead of the $300-600 the unmarked ones make.
patience: Moderate to high. Farm and school bells run regularly in New England sales.

analysis: An 18th-century pine settle bench with an integral lidded box in the seat, catalogued to the century, $800-1,200. The photograph is convincing: dry old red paint worn through to bare wood on the seat and arm exactly where a body wears it, dirt settled into the corners rather than sitting on the surface, boarded construction with shaped cut-out ends. This is one of the best genuine 18th-century objects in the whole sale on the evidence of a single image. It is also $1,056-1,584 all-in -- above the band -- and physically enormous.
problems: Above budget. Also a very large piece of furniture for a collection rather than a house-furnishing purchase. The catalogue says 'w/ game board' and no game board is visible in the first photograph; establish where it is and whether it is original or a later addition, because a painted game board on an 18th-c. settle would be a significant folk-art element and its absence is equally significant.
patience: Low. Period high-back settles in original paint are genuinely scarce -- this is a real object priced out of band, not a pass on merit.

analysis: Peter Q. Libbey (American/Maine, 1944-2018), carved eagle and serpent wall sculpture, $2,000-3,000. A documented Maine carver with a real regional following -- this is exactly the material the Maine criterion exists for, and it is the strongest Maine-maker sculpture in the sale. It is also $2,640-3,960 all-in, three to four times the band, and post-war by the artist's own dates so it earns nothing on age.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Maine carver prices are made almost entirely within Maine, which means a Thomaston sale is where they are highest, not lowest -- the room will be full of the right buyers.
patience: Moderate. Libbey carvings surface in Maine sales periodically.

analysis: A Napoleonic prisoner-of-war bone carving in the form of a spinning wheel, $1,000-1,500. POW bone work -- made by French prisoners in English hulks and depots from soup bones and scrap -- is a legitimate, documented and genuinely scarce category, comfortably pre-1926 and with a real collecting base. Bone rather than ivory, so none of the marine-mammal or elephant restrictions apply. $1,320-1,980 all-in puts it above the band.
problems: Above budget. POW bone work is also faked, both by 19th-century imitators and by modern makers, and the tells -- bone rather than ivory grain, hand-drilled pin holes, the particular economy of scrap-bone construction -- need magnification. Bone models are structurally fragile and losses are normal; count the spokes and the maidens. Only the catalogue's word on the date.
patience: Low. Genuine POW bone work is scarce and does not come through often.

spread: The range is an authentication question rather than a valuation one. A genuine Qing government seal with a readable Manchu-and-seal-script inscription and a real chop is a scholarly object; a modern cast copy of one is a $200 curio, and the photographs cannot separate them. No margin is shown because averaging that spread would be inventing a number.
analysis: A Chinese Qing bronze official seal with Manchu and seal-script inscriptions, $600-800. Bilingual Manchu-Chinese seals are a real category of Qing administrative material and an authentic one with a legible office inscription is a genuinely interesting scholarly object -- the inscription names a specific post, which makes it documentary rather than decorative. Inside the band at $792-1,056 all-in, just.
problems: Official seals are among the most reproduced Chinese bronzes, precisely because the inscription does the selling and a modern caster can copy an inscription. The things to check are whether the Manchu is actually correct Manchu rather than decorative pseudo-script, whether the chop face shows genuine ink and use wear, and whether the patina is grown or applied. This is a read-the-inscription problem, not a look-at-the-photograph problem -- it needs someone who can read Manchu, which the catalogue clearly did not have.
patience: Moderate. Chinese seals run regularly; genuine bilingual official ones do not.

analysis: A Chinese Kangxi gilt bronze fragment of a Confucian warrior sculpture, $1,000-1,500 -- above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in. The honesty of the word 'fragment' is worth noting; the house is not pretending this is complete.
problems: Above budget. A specific reign attribution on an unmarked bronze fragment is an assertion, and Kangxi is the reign name most freely applied to undated Chinese bronzes. Fragments are also where the provenance questions around Chinese architectural and religious sculpture concentrate.

analysis: A Chinese bronze ding, $700-900, with six photographs and no date anywhere in the title. Archaistic bronze ritual vessels have been cast in China continuously since the Song dynasty as scholarly revivals and since the 19th century for export; the modern ones are excellent. When a cataloguer photographs a piece six times and still writes no date, the photographs did not settle it for them either.
problems: No date, no inscription discussed, no provenance. Genuine archaic Chinese bronze is a licensing and provenance minefield as well as an authentication one. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band for something undated.

analysis: Two Chinese bronze hand mirrors, $200-300. Tang and Han-style bronze mirrors are the single most reproduced Chinese antiquity -- they are small, easy to cast from an original, and artificially patinated convincingly. Undated.
problems: No date, no discussion of patina or casting. Pairs of matching bronze mirrors surviving from any real antiquity is itself improbable. Estimate assumes an age nobody claims.

analysis: Three Chinese jade carvings, $250-350 -- one of two identically described lots (see 1343). Neither gives a date, a material specification beyond 'jade', or a subject.
problems: 'Jade' covers nephrite, jadeite, serpentine, bowenite and dyed quartzite, and the difference is an order of magnitude. Distinguishing them needs specific gravity and refractive index, not a photograph. No date. Two identical lots in one session.

analysis: Three Chinese jade carvings, $250-350 -- word for word the same as 1330, thirteen lots earlier. See that entry.
problems: Same as 1330, and competing directly with it.

analysis: A Chinese Shiwan porcelain figurine, $200-300. Shiwan ware from Guangdong is a genuine tradition and the 19th-century mudmen and immortals are collected, but the kilns have produced the same figures continuously to the present and the modern ones are abundant. Undated.
problems: No date, no mark. Estimate is above the undated market. One of two Shiwan lots (see 1349).

analysis: A Chinese Shiwan immortal figurine, $200-300. Second Shiwan lot; see 1337.
problems: Same as 1337.

analysis: A 'Roman STYLE' marble bust of a woman, $500-700. The word 'style' is the cataloguer declining to commit, and on classical sculpture that is the entire question. This is a Grand Tour or later decorative marble after an antique type -- a real category, but not an antiquity.
problems: 'Style' with no date and no carver. Decorative classical busts are produced in Italy in quantity today and aged convincingly. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band for something undated.

analysis: A 'Roman bronze bust of man', $1,000-1,500 -- and note that the neighbouring marble, 2425, gets the qualifier 'style' while this one does not. Dropping the qualifier without adding a date or a provenance, and raising the estimate, is the estimate implying something the words will not say. A genuine Roman bronze portrait bust is a museum object worth six or seven figures; this is not one.
problems: Above budget at $1,320-1,980 all-in. Antiquities also carry export-licence and provenance obligations that this catalogue does not address at all, and buying an unprovenanced 'Roman bronze' is a legal exposure as well as an authentication one. Treat this as a 19th-c. or later decorative bronze after the antique.

analysis: Five Indian and Himalayan bronze and soapstone figural objects, $300-500. A box lot of unspecified devotional figures with no date, no deity identified and no region beyond a subcontinent.
problems: Himalayan and Indian bronzes are made for the tourist and devotional market in enormous quantity and aged for sale. Nothing here is dated. Provenance questions attach to religious sculpture from this region.

analysis: A large Ottoman bronze pedestal brazier, $400-600. Ottoman and Persian brass and bronze braziers are made continuously for the decorative trade and the older ones are hard to separate from the newer without handling. Undated.
problems: No date. Large, heavy, and a shipping problem from Maine. Estimate is above the decorative market.

analysis: A polychrome enamelled Indian bronze of Shiva and Parvati, $1,000-1,500 -- above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in. Enamelled polychrome finishes on Indian bronzes are overwhelmingly a modern decorative treatment.
problems: Above budget. No date. Polychrome enamel is itself a modern-production signal. Religious sculpture provenance questions apply.

analysis: A pair of Steuben glass gazelle bookends, $500-700. Steuben's gazelle motif dates from Sidney Waugh's work of the mid-1930s and the bookends were produced for decades. Documented maker, post-1926, and in the market the standing brief names as having corrected hard without recovering.
problems: Steuben's secondary market is roughly a third of what it was fifteen years ago, and colourless mid-century Steuben is the weakest part of it. Estimate is well above current results. Check both bookends for chips at the bases, which is where they always go.
patience: Very high. Steuben appears in most decorative-arts sales.

analysis: An 'antique' bronze-mounted ceramic Easter egg box, $300-500. Egg-form gilt-metal-mounted porcelain boxes are a late-19th-century Continental form -- often French or Bohemian, sometimes in the Russian manner -- and a good one with intact hinges and original decoration is an attractive small object.
problems: 'Antique' with no date, no country and no maker is the cataloguer using the word as an adjective, not a claim. The egg form is also the single most-copied Russian and Continental decorative object because of the Faberge association, and modern gilt-metal-mounted eggs are everywhere. Check the hinge and clasp for period construction and the interior for a lining that matches the age of the shell.

analysis: A cast bronze house sign with a pheasant theme, $350-450. Undated architectural or garden cast work. A pleasant object with no age claim and no maker.
problems: No date, no maker. Decorative cast bronze signage is made new continuously. Estimate assumes an age nobody offers.

analysis: Black Forest walnut 'Don Quixote' bookends, $300-400. Black Forest carving -- the Brienz workshops of Switzerland, misnamed for the German region -- is a genuine and dateable tradition running from the mid-19th century to about 1930, and carved figural bookends are a real form. If period, this is a modest antique with a documented tradition behind it.
problems: 'Black Forest' is used loosely for any dark carved European woodwork, and Don Quixote as a subject points more to Spanish 20th-century tourist carving than to Brienz. No date. Check the carving quality and the back faces: genuine Brienz work is fully finished and finely undercut, tourist work is not.

analysis: A small cast stone sculpture signed 'Michel' on the base, $300-400. An unidentified signature -- the standing principle is explicit: the cataloguer saw a signature and could not identify it, so do not pay named-maker money for it. Cast stone is also a reproduction medium by definition.
problems: Unidentified single-name signature on a cast material. No date, no subject, no size. Estimate assumes the signature means something.

analysis: A pair of bronze urn-form wine buckets with liners, $800-1,200. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in. Handsome objects and the liners are a good sign of completeness, but undated.
problems: Above budget. No date, no maker, no country. Bronze and brass jardinieres and coolers in classical urn form are produced continuously; the liners could be original or later. Note the standing rule about liners: on a metal lot, glass or base-metal liners are deducted before any melt or metal reasoning, though bronze has no melt floor to speak of anyway.

analysis: A pair of French gilded bronze 'Warwick vase STYLE' urns, $400-600. The Warwick Vase is a specific antique marble in Glasgow and reduced bronze copies of it were a Grand Tour and Victorian staple; 'style' here means these are copies of copies. Undated.
problems: 'Style' plus no date. Gilded finishes on decorative bronze are frequently later regilding, which is invisible in a photograph and halves the value. Estimate is at the top of the market for undated decorative urns.

analysis: A bronze bull sculpture, $600-800 -- no artist, no date, no foundry, no size. One of four undated decorative animal bronzes across the sale (1180 bull, 3023 cow, 3018 bullfrog, 3173 lions), all in the same $600-1,500 band and all anonymous. That pattern is a decorator's consignment, not a sculpture consignment.
problems: No artist, no date, no foundry mark discussed. Anonymous animal bronzes are cast in quantity in Asia for the garden and interior trade and are routinely catalogued as though the absence of a signature were an open question. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.

analysis: A bronze cow sculpture, $800-1,200. See 1180 -- second of the anonymous animal bronzes. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget, no artist, no date, no foundry.

analysis: A bronze bullfrog garden fountainhead, $1,000-1,500. Third of the anonymous animal bronzes and the most clearly functional -- garden fountain figures are a decorative-trade staple made new in quantity. Above the band.
problems: Above budget at $1,320-1,980 all-in. No artist, no date. Fountain figures are usually plumbed, which means drilled, and outdoor exposure produces the green patina that reads as age.

analysis: A bronze sculpture of lions on a green marble base, $800-1,200. Fourth of the anonymous animal bronzes. A marble base is a mounting convention of 20th-century decorative casting rather than an age indicator. Above the band.
problems: Above budget. No artist, no date, no foundry. Anonymous.

analysis: A French bronze desk stand on a marble base, $800-1,000. Encriers and desk stands of this type are a genuine late-19th and early-20th-century Continental form and a good one is a satisfying object. Above the band at $1,056-1,320 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No date, no foundry. Desk stands are almost always missing their inkwell liners and their pen tray fittings -- count the components against the recesses. 'French' with no maker is a guess at origin.

analysis: A circa 1900 bronze and carved alabaster chandelier, $800-1,200. Catalogued to c.1900, so genuinely antique, and carved alabaster shades of that date are a real Continental form with Art Nouveau associations. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Alabaster chips and yellows and the shades are almost always replaced or repaired; check every element for matching stone and matching carving. Rewiring a period chandelier for modern use is a real cost. No maker.

analysis: An 'early' bronze figural chandelier, $700-900. 'Early' is the vaguest age word available and does no work. Figural bronze chandeliers span 1880 to the present with little visual change. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band.
problems: Above budget. No date, no maker, no country. Rewiring cost. Figural chandeliers are heavily reproduced.

analysis: A Tiffany Studios bronze harp floor lamp base, $2,000-3,000. The companion to 3051's Acorn shade, and the same conclusion: $2,640-3,960 all-in, three to four times the band. Genuine harp bases are stamped and numbered and do trade in this range.
problems: Above budget. Tiffany bases are reproduced and remounted constantly, and bases are frequently married to shades they never carried. Authentication needs the stamp, the number and the base's weighting examined in hand.
patience: Low on genuine Tiffany, irrelevant at this budget.

analysis: The description gives it a date and a subject, both of which I said were missing. 'CIRCA 1890 cast bronze, unsigned, PROBABLY FRENCH, having a Writhing Nude Woman grasping the rim of an oversized Pirate's Head from behind, tricorn crown providing the pouring spout, also having high relief and chased decoration of flowering branches'. So it is catalogued as antique, and the subject is genuinely extraordinary -- a symbolist grotesque rather than the generic 'Art Nouveau pitcher' the title suggests. The date makes the Art Nouveau criterion arguable rather than empty, since c.1890 is the movement's actual period.
problems: Above the band at $2,640-3,960 all-in, which is why this remains a pass. Still unsigned and with no foundry mark, so 'probably French' is as far as the attribution goes and there is no name to underwrite the price. Symbolist bronzes of this kind were also cast well into the 20th century from original models. At $2,000-3,000 the house is asking period money on a period claim it will not sign.
patience: High. Nouveau-style bronze is everywhere; genuine signed period work is not, and it is not this.

analysis: A Paolo Soleri (Italian-American, 1919-2013) Arcosanti bronze windbell, $600-800. Soleri is a documented and significant figure and the Arcosanti bells are genuinely his design, sand-cast at the Cosanti and Arcosanti foundries -- but they have been made continuously since the 1960s, are still sold new today, and the secondary market for the standard bells is $150-450.
problems: Estimate is well above the secondary market for a still-in-production object. Post-1926 by a long way. Establish whether this is one of the larger or earlier assemblies, which are the only ones that break $500, and look for the Soleri signature stamp.
patience: Very high -- you can buy one new.

analysis: A Chilmark limited-edition McGrory Native American sculpture, $800-1,200. Chilmark was a Rhode Island producer of limited-edition pewter and cold-cast figures sold through the collectibles market of the 1980s and 90s. That market collapsed completely and these resell for a small fraction of their original retail.
problems: Estimate is roughly ten times the secondary market. 'Limited edition' in the collectibles trade means an edition of thousands. Post-1926 by decades and no criteria fit whatever.

analysis: A life-sized resin bird sculpture, $300-500. Resin is a modern material and the catalogue says so plainly. Decorative.
problems: Modern material, no maker, no date. Estimate is above the decorative market.

analysis: A carved stone mermaid sculpture attributed to 'Wilerid Ciricus', $500-700. That name does not correspond to any documented sculptor and reads as a garbled transcription of a signature -- add it to the list of cataloguing errors in this sale. Per the standing principle, an unidentified signature is speculative and this one has not even been transcribed reliably.
problems: The artist's name as printed appears to be wrong. No date, no stone identified. A mermaid subject is decorative and, in Maine, a commercial one.

analysis: A 'cubist marble sculpture of lovers', $1,000-1,500. Cubism as a movement ran 1907-1920s; a sculpture described only by style with no artist and no date is a later work in the manner. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget, no artist, no date. A style name substituting for an attribution.

analysis: An abstract metal sculpture, artist unknown, $300-500. The catalogue is entirely candid: nobody knows who made it. Anonymous mid-century modern metal sculpture has a decorative market and no collector market.
problems: 'Artist unknown' in the title. No date, no material, no size. Estimate assumes decorator demand.

analysis: A 'balanced woman' steel sculpture, $800-1,200. No artist, no date. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget, anonymous, undated, modern material.

analysis: A Canadian folk art carving of a teamster, $300-400. Quebec folk carving is a real and collected tradition with named makers -- Caron, Bourgault, Cote and the Saint-Jean-Port-Joli workshops -- and a good painted figure with movement is an appealing object. Anonymous here, and almost certainly 20th century.
problems: No maker, no date, no province. Saint-Jean-Port-Joli produced enormous quantities of carved figures for the tourist trade from the 1930s onward, and separating a genuine folk carving from a workshop souvenir is a matter of surface and individuality rather than any mark. Estimate is at the top of the anonymous market.
patience: High. Quebec carvings run regularly in New England sales.

analysis: A 19th-century French ivory figurine, $650-750. Genuinely antique by the catalogue's own dating, and Dieppe and Continental ivory carving of the period is a real tradition -- but this is elephant ivory, and that changes the calculation entirely. Federal law and a number of state laws including Maine's restrict ivory commerce, and the antique exemptions require documentary proof of age that this lot does not offer. Buying it means owning something you cannot lawfully resell.
problems: Ivory with no age documentation. The resale figure is zero: not a judgement on the carving, but the practical reality that an undocumented ivory cannot be sold on. For a collector who asks 'if I ever had to let it go, what do I lose?', the answer here is all of it. One of three ivory lots in the sale (see 2401, 2489).
patience: Not applicable -- this is a category to avoid.

analysis: A 19th-century German ivory figurine, $750-850 -- the second ivory lot and the same answer as 2355. Erbach and Bavarian ivory carving is a documented tradition and the date is catalogued, but no documentation of age accompanies the lot, which is what the law requires.
problems: Ivory, undocumented. Zero resale for the reasons set out at 2355. Above the comfortable band as well, at $990-1,122 all-in.

analysis: An early 20th-century Chinese ivory doctor's doll, $300-400 -- the reclining figures physicians supposedly used so that women could indicate symptoms without examination. A genuine and interesting object type, catalogued to the early 20th century so straddling the antique line. Third ivory lot in the sale and the same conclusion.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale. 'Early 20th century' also puts it either side of 1926 with no way to tell, which matters legally as well as for the age criterion. Doctor's dolls are additionally one of the most reproduced Chinese ivory forms, made in quantity for export from the 1920s onward and still made in bone and resin today.

analysis: Closed, and cleanly. The description says the case has five drawers containing BONE AND BAMBOO tiles, blank tiles, coins and scoring sticks -- bone laminated to bamboo, which is the good grade of 1920s set and carries none of the ivory restrictions. That was the material question and it was a legal one as well as a value one; it is answered. A brass-mounted wooden case with a slide-out lid inscribed with Chinese characters, five drawers, and the counters and sticks present, catalogued to the 1920s, at $300-500 is a complete period set inside the band.
problems: Still count the tiles at preview -- 144 for a standard set, and the catalogue's mention of 'blank tiles' is ambiguous between spare blanks (good) and replacements (less good). Bone-and-bamboo tiles separate at the glue line with age and humidity; check a few. The 1920s dating puts it right on the antique line, so this is a border lot rather than a clear antique. Brass mounts on these cases tarnish and the lid slides bind.
patience: Moderate. Mahjong sets run regularly but complete cased 1920s ones are the better share.

analysis: Six Halloween decorations by H.E. Luhrs, $200-300 -- the first of a five-lot Halloween consignment (1182-1186). H.E. Luhrs of Shippensburg, Pennsylvania produced diecut Halloween decorations from the 1930s to the 1950s, which makes 'antique' in the title wrong: this is mid-century, not pre-1926. Vintage Halloween is a genuinely hot collecting field with real prices, so the estimates here are not fantasy -- they simply buy something that fails the age criterion.
problems: Catalogued as 'antique' when the maker's production window is 1930s-50s. Diecut paper is fragile and condition drives everything; six pieces means six condition problems. No criteria fit.
patience: High. Vintage Halloween runs constantly, especially in autumn sales.

analysis: Three 'antique' Halloween lanterns, $300-400 -- the best lot in the Halloween consignment. German pulp and composition jack-o'-lantern lanterns of roughly 1910-1930 are the top of the vintage Halloween market and genuinely can predate 1926; the American pulp ones are 1940s-50s and much cheaper. Three lanterns at $100-135 each is honest pricing if they are the German ones, and cheap if any is early.
problems: German versus American is the entire question and the title does not address it. German lanterns have paper inserts, a wire bail and a distinctive coarse pulp; American ones are smoother and lighter. Paper inserts are almost always missing -- an intact original insert doubles a lantern. Composition pulp crumbles and is easily restored invisibly.
patience: Moderate. Early German Halloween lanterns are the scarce end of a well-supplied field.

analysis: I passed this as undated mid-century paper. The description dates every piece and two of them clear the antique line: 'German Devil in Flames, CA 1900, 19" x 8"; German Howling Black Cat Head, CA 1920, 12" x 14"; H. E. Luhrs Skull & Cross Bones, ca 1930 ... H. E. Luhrs Black Cat Head'. Early German embossed papier-mache and cardboard Halloween is the top of the vintage Halloween market -- well above the American Luhrs material of the 1930s-50s that makes up the rest of this consignment -- and a 19-inch c.1900 German Devil is a significant piece in that field on its own. This is the one lot in the five-lot Halloween block worth pursuing.
problems: Mixed lot: two early German pieces carrying the value, the rest 1930s Luhrs at $30-60 each. Embossed papier-mache and cardboard is fragile and these are large -- expect edge chips, creases, fading and old tape repairs, and the cellophane on the Luhrs skull will have yellowed and split. Condition drives everything in this category and the catalogue says nothing about it. Border rather than antique because only part of the lot predates 1926.
patience: Moderate. American vintage Halloween is deep supply; early German diecuts are not.

analysis: Six 'antique' Halloween decorations, $250-350. Same consignment, same window, same objection as 1184.
problems: No maker, no date, mid-century material described as antique.

analysis: Two 'antique' Halloween games plus napkins and a card, $200-300. The tail of the Halloween consignment -- paper party goods, which is the most fragile and least valuable end of the category.
problems: Paper party goods, mid-century, described as antique. Estimate is above the market.

analysis: Twelve bisque Kewpie dolls, $300-500. Rose O'Neill's Kewpies were produced in German bisque from 1913 and the early ones carry the O'Neill signature on the foot and a paper heart label on the chest -- and those genuinely predate 1926. Twelve pieces at $25-40 each is a fair number for a mixed group, and the better single examples in a lot like this can be worth more than the estimate on their own.
problems: 'Vintage' rather than dated, and Kewpies were reproduced in Japanese bisque from the 1920s and in every material since. The tells are the O'Neill signature on the sole, the mould crispness, and the blue wings. Twelve small bisque figures means chips and hairlines; assume some are damaged. Sort the group at preview -- the value is in one or two pieces, not twelve.
patience: High. Kewpies are abundant; signed early German ones less so.

analysis: The description narrows the date and adds the damage. 'Vintage Painted Wood and Metal Horse and Dairy Delivery Wagon, by Illinois maker Rich Toys (1921-34), with driver figure and pull cord.' The 1921-34 window straddles the antique line, so this is border rather than modern -- but the rest of the description is why it stays a pass.
problems: 'Missing horse tail and milk bottles; modifications to delivery wagon.' The milk bottles are the whole charm of a dairy wagon and they are gone; 'modifications' on a toy means somebody has altered it, which is worse than wear. Lithographed and painted wood toys live or die on originality and this one has lost both parts and integrity.

analysis: Two 'early' cast iron and pressed steel toys, $200-300. Cast iron toys of 1900-1930 -- Hubley, Arcade, Kenton, Dent -- are a genuine antique category and the earlier ones clear 1926 comfortably. Two toys at $100-150 each is reasonable if they are period.
problems: Cast iron toys are the most reproduced antique toy category in existence; the reproductions have been made since the 1950s and the tells are casting crispness, seam fit, screw type and the weight and colour of the paint. Neither toy is named or dated. 'Early' does no work.

analysis: Two 1930s tin model train buildings, Lionel and Marklin, $200-300. Both are documented and important makers and the date is catalogued -- but 1930s is post-1926, and tinplate accessory buildings are the least valuable part of the train market.
problems: Post-1926 by the catalogue's own dating. Tinplate accessories rust and the lithography fades; condition drives the price and no condition information is given. No catalogue numbers, which is how this material is actually valued.

analysis: A 1950s Doepke Model Toys Caterpillar D6 bulldozer, $200-300. Doepke pressed-steel construction toys are genuinely collected and the D6 is one of the better models. Catalogued to the decade, so unambiguously modern.
problems: Post-1926 by three decades. Doepke value depends heavily on original paint, complete tracks and the presence of the box, none of which is mentioned. No criteria fit.

analysis: A rosewood-cased mother-of-pearl dominoes set, $200-300. Nineteenth-century gaming sets in fitted rosewood cases are genuinely antique and the mother-of-pearl-faced dominoes -- usually pearl over ebony, pinned together with brass -- are the good grade. A complete cased set is an attractive small object with real age.
problems: Count the tiles against the case recesses; incomplete sets are worth a fraction, and the standing rule about cased sets applies directly. The backs are usually ebony and the pins brass, but some sets use bone rather than pearl and some use ivory, which would raise the same legal issue as the ivory lots elsewhere in this sale -- confirm at preview. No date offered.
patience: High. Cased Victorian gaming sets run regularly.

analysis: A Cor-Cor Toys pressed steel Chrysler Airflow car, $300-500. Cor-Cor of Washington, Indiana made large pressed-steel Airflows in the late 1930s and they are among the more desirable American pressed-steel toys -- a genuine Deco design in a genuine Deco form. Post-1926, so no age criterion, but the estimate is roughly right for the market.
problems: Post-1926. Cor-Cor Airflows are also reproduced, and repainted originals are common; original paint is worth several times a restoration. No condition information given.
patience: Moderate. Cor-Cor Airflows appear in toy sales a few times a year.

analysis: A German hide-covered horse and cart pull toy, $700-900. Hide-covered horses on wheeled platforms are a genuine late-19th and early-20th-century German nursery form -- real horsehide over a papier-mache or wood body, with glass eyes and often a leather harness -- and they clear 1926 comfortably. The best lot in the Day 1 toy consignment on age, and a handsome object. At $924-1,188 all-in it sits just above the comfortable band.
problems: Just above budget at the estimate. Hide-covered toys are exceptionally vulnerable: the hide dries, splits and sheds, moths eat it, and the mane and tail are almost always replaced. The wheeled platform and cart are frequently married from separate toys. Three photographs, none of which will show the underside of the hide.
patience: Moderate. German hide-covered horses run regularly but complete horse-and-cart combinations are the smaller share.

analysis: A four-piece folk art kinetic toy collection, $200-300 -- one of two adjacent lots (see 1210). Whittled moving toys -- whimsies, whirligigs, jointed figures, sawyers and hammer men -- are a real folk-art category with genuine collector interest when the surface and invention are right.
problems: No date, no maker, no region, and the category spans a century with no visual break. Folk toys are also made now, deliberately aged, and sold as old. Judge on wear at the moving joints and the coherence of the paint. Two adjacent lots means they compete with each other.

analysis: A five-piece folk art kinetic toy collection, $200-300 -- companion to 1208, one more piece for the same money. See that entry.
problems: Same as 1208, and directly competing with it in the same session.

analysis: A 'rare vintage sea griffin carousel figure', $3,000-5,000. Carousel figures are a real and expensive collecting field -- a documented Dentzel, Looff or Illions menagerie figure is a five-figure object -- and a sea griffin is an unusual form. It is also $3,960-6,600 all-in, four to six times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. 'Vintage' with no carver, no date and no park provenance is the whole problem: carousel figures are reproduced in fibreglass and in carved wood for the decorator trade, and repainted originals are the norm. At this estimate the carver needs to be established and is not.

analysis: A vintage Jennings 'Standard Chief' slot machine, $1,000-2,000. Jennings Standard Chiefs date from the mid-1930s to the 1940s and are a genuine and active collecting field with good Deco casework. Post-1926 and above the band at $1,320-2,640 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Slot machines are also regulated: several states restrict private ownership of gambling devices, and while Maine permits antique machines over 25 years old, this is worth confirming before bidding. Restored versus original casework and mechanism is most of the value and nothing is said about either.
patience: Moderate. Slot machines run regularly in Americana sales.

analysis: A Mills Novelty Art Deco Club Bell slot machine, $2,000-3,000. The Mills Deco-cased machines are the design high point of the category and the estimate reflects a real market. $2,640-3,960 all-in, three to four times the band.
problems: Above budget. Same regulatory point as 3028. Mills castings are reproduced and 'restored' machines frequently mix new castings with old mechanisms.

analysis: A food vendor trailer, $5,000-10,000. A working commercial asset, not a collectable. Six to ten times the band and outside every criterion.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Commercial equipment with licensing, inspection and towing considerations none of which belong in this analysis.

analysis: A 2007 Mercedes C-Class sedan, $4,000-6,000. A used car. Nineteen years old, four to six times the band, no criteria fit.
problems: A running vehicle sold at auction with no service history, inspection or mileage given here. Not a collection purchase.

analysis: A 2000 BMW Z3 M Roadster convertible, $15,000-20,000 -- the highest-estimated lot in this group and one of the highest in the sale. The M Roadster is a genuinely appreciating modern classic and the estimate is if anything conservative, but it is fifteen to twenty times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. Modern-classic car values depend entirely on mileage, service history and the S52 engine's condition, none of which is here.

analysis: A 2007 Mercedes S-Class S 550 4Matic sedan, $6,000-8,000. A used car, six to eight times the band.
problems: Above budget, no criteria fit. Nineteen-year-old S-Class running costs are a well-known trap in their own right.

analysis: A Wilderness Systems Tsunami 145 kayak, $800-1,200. Current-production recreational equipment. Genuinely useful in midcoast Maine and completely outside every collecting criterion.
problems: Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in, and a used kayak retails below that. Buy this from a paddling shop, not at 25% premium plus tax.

analysis: An Alumacraft Quetico 17 canoe, $400-600. Aluminium recreational canoe, current or recent production. No criteria fit; the estimate is roughly the used market and the premium takes it above it.
problems: At $528-792 all-in you are paying above the private-sale price for a used aluminium canoe. Not a collection object.

analysis: A Champion 27-ton log splitter, $1,000-1,500. Current-production machinery.
problems: Above the band, and a new one costs about the same. Not a collection object.

analysis: A 1966 Volkswagen Beetle (Type 1) 1300, $15,000-20,000 -- one of two lots in the sale with no lot number in the catalogue data. The 1966 1300 is a desirable single-year model and the estimate is in the market for a good one. Fifteen to twenty times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. Beetle values are entirely about rust in the heater channels and pan, which no photograph shows and no catalogue here describes. No lot number means no straightforward way to bid online.
